summary: This memo collects personal reflections on the 2013 disclosures about the US National Security Agency made by Edward Snowden, and on what happened afterward. It offers four viewpoints: someone who helped sift the material for responsible publication, an IETF security area director, a human rights expert, and a computer science and law professor. It aims to give historical perspective and views on future security and privacy work.

plainLanguage.summary: Years ago a secret was spilled about people being watched online. Four grown-ups tell what they saw and learned, so everyone remembers it and builds safer things next time.

questions: what did the ietf do after snowden
how has internet security improved since 2013
subtitle: Four perspectives on ten years since the NSA surveillance revelations

tldr.problem: Edward Snowden's 2013 disclosures revealed the extent of NSA surveillance, shocking the Internet technical community and raising urgent questions about privacy, security, and government oversight of communications.
tldr.mechanism: Four experts offer personal reflections: Bruce Schneier on his experience reading the classified documents, Stephen Farrell on the IETF's technical response, Farzaneh Badii on human rights implications, and Steven Bellovin on the historical context of cryptography and government control.
tldr.outcome: A decade later, the technical community has made significant progress on encryption and privacy, but broader surveillance capitalism remains largely unaddressed, and government cryptography restrictions persist.

today: RFC 9446 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023 and remains an Internet Standard. It does not define any protocols or requirements but serves as a historical record of perspectives ten years after Edward Snowden's 2013 disclosures about NSA surveillance. The document stands as testimony to how a single person's actions can catalyze global changes in how the technical community thinks about privacy and security.

sections.title: The Snowden Revelations and Their Significance
sections.content:
In June 2013, The Guardian published the first article revealing that the United States National Security Agency (NSA) conducted massive surveillance operations on communications worldwide. Edward Snowden, a contractor working for the NSA, had leaked thousands of classified documents to journalists including Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras. These disclosures shocked the Internet technical community by confirming, in unprecedented detail, the scope and methods of pervasive monitoring that many had suspected but never seen documented.

The revelations included secret court orders, agreements for bulk collection of communications metadata, tapping of undersea cables, and detailed descriptions of surveillance programs with code names like PRISM and QUANTUM. The sheer scale of these activities—far beyond anything the public understood to be technically feasible—catalyzed a global conversation about privacy, security, and the proper balance between government power and individual freedom. This memo collects the personal reflections of four key figures who grappled with these questions in the decade that followed.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret was revealed: the government was listening to way more phone calls and reading more emails than anyone thought. This made people very upset and worried about privacy, so engineers started working to fix it.

sections.title: Bruce Schneier's Personal Account of Reading the Documents
sections.content:
Bruce Schneier, a renowned security expert, was invited by journalist Glenn Greenwald to Rio de Janeiro to help interpret the technical contents of the Snowden archive. Schneier's essay offers a remarkable first-hand narrative of the experience: the surreal nature of paging through top-secret NSA documents, the mundane operational details alongside shocking revelations, and the psychological toll of exposure to classified information. He describes how reading about the NSA's hacking capabilities made him profoundly doubt his own security procedures, even for a security professional.

Schneier witnessed both the care taken by Greenwald and The Guardian to redact information responsibly and the extraordinary scope of what the NSA had collected. He notes that Snowden himself was careful to prevent the most harmful materials from being released. Yet the experience revealed that any person with sufficient access could exfiltrate massive amounts of classified material with relatively little accountability—what Schneier calls "the greatest intelligence failure in the history of ever." His reflections underscore the tension between the technical community's theoretical knowledge of surveillance possibilities and the shock of seeing them confirmed in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: One security expert got to read secret NSA documents and was amazed at how much the government had built to watch people. He felt scared about his own computer security after learning what was possible.

sections.title: The IETF's Technical and Policy Response
sections.content:
Stephen Farrell, who served as the IETF's security area director, documents the technical community's organized response to the revelations. Within months of the June 2013 disclosures, the IETF established new mailing lists, organized special sessions, and by May 2014 published RFC 7258, which declared that "pervasive monitoring is a technical attack" that should be mitigated in protocol design. This was a remarkable statement: the IETF, a standards body focused on technical specifications, took an explicit policy stance against mass surveillance.

The response catalyzed substantial technical work: development of TLS 1.3 with better encryption of handshakes, standardization of DNS encryption (DoT and DoH), widespread deployment of HTTPS via Let's Encrypt, and emphasis on removing long-term identifiers that enable tracking. Farrell notes that over 90 percent of email between mail servers is now encrypted, and security considerations are now front-and-center in protocol design. However, he observes that the technical community has done less well against "surveillance capitalism"—the business model of data collection by large technology companies—largely because such practices operate outside the scope of protocol standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers who make Internet standards met and decided that spying on everyone was bad. They made new rules for how the Internet should work to make it harder to listen in on people.

sections.title: Human Rights Implications and Global Impact
sections.content:
Farzaneh Badii, a human rights expert, examines whether the Snowden revelations actually improved Internet-based human rights. She concludes that while the revelations helped expedite technical solutions like encrypted DNS and RDAP (which protects domain registrant privacy), they have not fundamentally shifted how the technical community balances human rights. The IETF has not yet adopted a comprehensive human-rights-centered approach to protocol design, and deployment of human-rights-enabling technologies remains hindered by regulatory and market factors outside the IETF's control.

Badii highlights tensions in the human rights space: encryption protects privacy and freedom of expression but may complicate law enforcement access to prevent crime; DNS encryption reduces surveillance but can hamper child protection efforts; and technical solutions cannot address political or regulatory barriers to implementation. She argues that the technical community needs deeper engagement with rights impact assessments and must acknowledge that protocols operate within complex social, legal, and economic contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: A human rights expert looked at whether the changes made people safer. The answer is: some things got better, but the world is complicated, and not everything engineers fix helps everyone equally.

sections.title: Cryptography, Government Policy, and the Ongoing Conflict
sections.content:
Steven Bellovin provides historical context for the Snowden revelations, tracing government and private-sector use of cryptography back centuries. He shows that the modern "Crypto Wars"—government attempts to restrict or backdoor encryption—are not new. From DES key length reduction in the 1970s to the Clipper chip debate of the 1990s to post-Snowden disclosures about the DUAL_EC_DRBG random number generator containing an NSA backdoor, governments have repeatedly tried to weaken cryptography while maintaining their own capabilities.

Bellovin notes that despite the Snowden revelations, governments including the US, UK, and Australia continue to push for encryption restrictions or backdoors justified by law enforcement and national security arguments. He emphasizes that the IETF's commitment to strong, ubiquitous encryption remains essential but insufficient: protocols must also maintain "cryptoagility" to upgrade to stronger algorithms as quantum computing threatens current methods, protect metadata (which General Michael Hayden notes can be used to kill people), and address the reality that SIGINT agencies will not disappear. The fundamental challenge is designing systems that are secure against both government overreach and criminal threats.
sections.plainLanguage: One computer scientist shows that governments have been trying to control codes and secret messages for hundreds of years. The fight between freedom and government power never really ends—it just changes form.

sections.title: Ten Years Later: Progress and Remaining Challenges
sections.content:
The four authors collectively paint a picture of mixed progress. The technical community succeeded in making encryption far more common—HTTPS is now the norm for web traffic, TLS protects most connections, and DNS encryption is gaining adoption. The IETF's RFC 7258 declaration that pervasive monitoring is an attack has been cited in hundreds of subsequent RFCs and working group charters. However, Farrell notes that the "real annoyance" felt toward government surveillance a decade ago is not felt nearly as acutely regarding commercial surveillance by tech companies, even though the data-collection practices are often more pervasive and privacy-invasive.

Bellovin warns that the Snowden documents are now over a decade old, that the NSA has rebuilt its capabilities, and that post-quantum cryptography will require significant protocol changes in coming years. The technical community has learned to design for privacy from the ground up, but much deployment work remains. The authors collectively suggest that Internet engineers must place greater emphasis on ethical standards and human rights implications in their work, while acknowledging that regulatory solutions may ultimately be necessary to address systemic problems that protocols alone cannot solve.
sections.plainLanguage: After ten years, the Internet got more encrypted and safer. But new problems came: big companies now collect data the way governments do. The fight for privacy is still going, and it's not just about technology anymore.
